summary: Thunderstorm safety for ages 5–7: children learn a short, correct set of safety rules (go inside a building or a hard-topped car; stay away from tall trees, open ground, and water such as pools, ponds and the sea), each paired with a child-level reason (lightning tends to hit the tallest thing around, and being on open ground or in or near water leaves you exposed; a building or hard-topped car carries lightning around you into the ground), plus calm emotional reassurance that storms are natural and following simple rules helps keep you safe. The core activity is rehearsing the decision 'hear thunder → go inside', complemented by a safe/unsafe place sort to confirm the rules. This is PSHE/personal-safety content; the thunder/lightning science is a later topic.
misconceptions: 'Shelter under a tree to stay dry/safe' — a dangerous myth; trees are among the worst places in a thunderstorm.
'Thunder can hurt you' — thunder is only the SOUND; the danger is lightning, and being indoors protects you.
'Water is fine to be in/near during a storm' — pools, ponds and the sea are unsafe; get out and away from water.
'If you can't see rain it's safe' — lightning can strike from a storm that's still some distance away; go in when you hear thunder.
'Storms are out to get you / are a punishment' — animistic fear; storms are natural, and simple rules keep you safe.

activities.title: Storm scenario: choose where to go
steps: Watch or imagine a storm rolling in — dark clouds gather and a rumble of thunder sounds.
Choose where to go: a house, a car, under a big tree, an open field, or beside a swimming pool.
When you choose a safe place (house or car), see yourself safe and cosy indoors, watching the storm from a little way back from the window.
When you choose an unsafe place, read the kind, un-scary prompt explaining why it is risky (e.g. 'a tall tree is one of the riskiest places — let's get inside instead') and try again.
Repeat the 'hear thunder → go inside' decision several times until it feels familiar.
activities.insight: Staying safe in a storm is a decision you can make and rehearse: go indoors or into a car, and the right action becomes familiar so you feel in control rather than frightened.

activities.title: Safe place / unsafe place sort
steps: Sort places and things into 'safe in a storm' and 'not safe in a storm'.
Safe: inside a building, inside a hard-topped car.
Unsafe: under a tall tree, in an open field, in or beside a swimming pool, pond or the sea.
For each one, say the reason aloud — e.g. 'a tall tree is unsafe because lightning tends to hit tall things'.
activities.insight: A tree is for rain shelter, not storm safety; the safe places are indoors or a car, and open or wet places are dangerous.

activities.title: Calm reassurance: thunder is just a sound
steps: Look at a scene of a child safe indoors, watching a storm from inside.
Hear or read the message that thunder is just a loud sound — it can't hurt you, but hearing it means lightning is near; the thing to stay away from is lightning, and being indoors protects you.
Talk about how storms are natural events, not something out to get you, and that knowing what to do helps you feel safe.
Optionally ask a caring, reassuring character a worry such as 'is thunder going to hurt me?' and talk through what to do.
activities.insight: Storms can feel scary because they are loud, but thunder is only the sound; following simple rules helps keep you safe, so you can feel in control.

activities.title: What should you do? quick check
steps: Answer: 'What should you do when you hear thunder?' — choosing 'go inside a building or car' over unsafe options.
Explain in your own words why indoors is safer than being out in the open.
Name one more thing to stay away from (tall trees, open ground, or water).
activities.insight: You can state at least two thunderstorm safety rules and say why indoors is safest.

checkQuestion: A big thunderstorm with lightning starts while you're playing in the park. A child says, 'Let's stand under that big tall tree to stay safe.' Is that a good idea? What should you do instead, and why?
checkAnswer: No — a tall tree is one of the most dangerous places to be in lightning, because lightning tends to strike the tallest thing around. You should go indoors or into a car, and stay away from trees and water. That keeps you away from where lightning is most likely to hit.
